766	\subsection{Extended Discussion}
767	\label{app:extended_discussion}
768	
769	\paragraph{Cross-strategy conditional decomposition.}
770	The two-stage pipeline (strategy identification followed by depth classification) recovers 11.5\,pp over the na\"ive pooled classifier.
771	Under correct strategy routing, four-class accuracy reaches 72.6\% vs.\ 68.0\% under misrouting ($N{=}103{,}498$ / $76{,}502$), a gap of 4.6\,pp; d0 accuracy remains near-ceiling (${\sim}99.6$\%) regardless of routing, confirming that the d0 signal is strategy-invariant.
772	Even the worst routing yields a floor of 67.6\% ($2.7\times$ chance), and the 31.5\,pp d1--d3 gap between correct and wrong routing confirms feature-space misalignment rather than uniform noise.
773	End-to-end PLMs lag RF by ${\sim}20$\,pp, suggesting that current pretrained representations do not capture the distributional tail statistics that drive depth discrimination.
774	
775	\paragraph{Depth-graduated curation.}
776	Current data curation operates on a binary human-vs-machine distinction \cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}.
777	Recursive generation depth estimation enables a finer-grained alternative: retain low-depth generations (d1) whose distributional properties remain close to the human source, while down-weighting or filtering high-depth text (d3+) where tail erosion has degraded quality.
778	The 70--85\% in-distribution accuracy and $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}4$ suggest depth-graduated filtering is feasible within known model--strategy configurations, though the d1/d2 boundary inversion under cross-strategy transfer (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}) means reliable curation requires either known decoding strategy metadata or an upstream strategy-identification step; a pilot study (Appendix~\ref{app:curation_poc}) yields an inconclusive RF-vs-unfiltered comparison ($p>0.4$), though RF-filtered subsets significantly outperform size-matched random subsampling ($p<0.001$--$0.02$); large-scale validation remains open.
779	Importance weighting \cite{sugiyama2007_importance_weighting} could further enable continuous depth-aware data selection rather than discrete thresholding.
780	
781	\paragraph{Toward a provenance toolkit.}
782	Depth estimation complements existing provenance methods along orthogonal axes.
783	Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} provides high-confidence attribution when the generator cooperates but is inapplicable to unwatermarked text.
784	Source attribution \cite{uchendu2020_attribution} identifies the generating model but not the generation history.
785	Depth estimation characterizes \emph{iterative reuse} regardless of generator cooperation or identity.
786	A layered provenance system combining these three signals (watermark presence, source model, and recursive generation depth) could support more nuanced data auditing than any single method.
787	
788	\subsection{Computational Resources and Reproducibility}
789	\label{app:compute}
790	
791	\paragraph{Hardware.}
792	All experiments were conducted on 2$\times$ NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (48\,GB) GPUs locally and 2$\times$ NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (48\,GB) on cloud instances.
793	Total computation is approximately 200 GPU$\cdot$hours, covering the $3 \times 3$ generation matrix (LoRA fine-tuning + sampling at each depth), feature extraction, depth extension to d5, 7--14B QLoRA experiments, and all ablations.
794	
795	\paragraph{Software.}
796	Key library versions: PyTorch 2.10.0+cu128, Transformers 5.8.1, PEFT 0.7.1, scikit-learn 1.8.0.
797	Additional dependencies: Accelerate 1.13.0, Datasets 4.8.4, XGBoost 3.2.0, NumPy 2.2.6 (Python 3.12.3, CUDA 12.8).
798	
799	\paragraph{Hyperparameters.}
800	LoRA hyperparameters ($r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, dropout $0.05$, lr $2{\times}10^{-4}$, batch size 8, 3 epochs) follow \citet{hu2022lora}.
801	The Random Forest classifier uses 200 trees, Gini criterion, and no max depth, without hyperparameter search; all reported results use 5-fold stratified cross-validation.
802	
803	\paragraph{Inference cost.}
804	Feature extraction and classification require no GPU.
805	Inference takes approximately 2 minutes per 5{,}000 samples on a single CPU core (reference-model forward pass + RF prediction), enabling deployment without specialized hardware.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding ACL ARR 2025-2026 reviewer guidelines, review form criteria, and scoring:

## Scoring System

Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation.

### Soundness Score
The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review. If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it.

### Excitement Score
Subjective preferences should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper.

## Area Chair Metareview Score

The ARR metareview score has changed in February 2025 to be more aligned with reviewer scores. Like with reviews, the score should be backed up by the meta-review text. The new metareview options include:
- 5 = Consider for Award: I think this paper could be considered for an outstanding paper award at an *ACL conference (up to top 2.5% papers).
- 2 = Resubmit next cycle: I think this paper needs substantial revisions that can be completed by the next ARR cycle.
- 1.5 = Resubmit after next cycle: I think this paper needs substantial revisions that cannot be completed by the next ARR cycle.
- 1 = Do not resubmit: This paper has to be fully redone, or it is not relevant to the *ACL community (e.g. it is in no way related to computational processing of language).

All reviewers must familiarize themselves with the latest version of the ARR reviewer guidelines and perform the reviews on time and in line with ARR requirements.

input.prompt: Extract the complete review form criteria, scoring dimensions (soundness, excitement, overall assessment), their scales, and detailed descriptions of each score level. Also extract any specific guidance on what constitutes a good vs bad review.

content.content:
# ARR Review Form Criteria and Guidance

## Scoring Dimensions

The guidelines specify **three distinct scores** that reviewers must provide:

1. **Soundness**: Technical validity and methodological rigor
2. **Excitement**: Personal interest and subjective appeal
3. **Overall Assessment**: Explicit recommendation for venue acceptance

## Soundness Score Guidance

The document emphasizes that "soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review." Low soundness ratings require clear deficiencies in the paper. Reviewers should examine whether they're relying on unconscious bias rather than substantive flaws.

## Excitement vs. Soundness

These are explicitly **orthogonal dimensions**. A reviewer may find work technically sound but personally uninteresting. Conversely, exciting work must still meet soundness standards. The guidance notes: "Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score."

## Overall Assessment

This composite score reflects "soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact." Importantly, papers can merit main conference acceptance even if reviewers aren't personally excited, particularly for high-quality resources or efficiency improvements with significant community impact.

## Key Characteristics of Strong Reviews

**Good reviews are**:
- Specific with referenced details
- Professional and neutral in tone
- Justified in their scoring
- Acknowledging of author responses

**Problematic reviews avoid**:
- Vague criticisms without examples
- Dismissive or sarcastic language
- Unjustified low scores
- Ignoring author clarifications

value.aiTitle: EMNLP 2026 Round 1 review for recursive generation depth estimation paper

content.thinking:
Now I have all the information needed for a thorough review. Let me compile the reference verification summary:

**Reference summary:**
- 68 bib entries, 67 cited (1 orphan: c2pa2024)
- 56 verified, 7 not found, 5 mismatch
- Not found: knowledge_collapse2025, falahati2026_curated, mitchell2023_detectgpt (but this is a very well-known paper), liu2019_roberta (also very well-known), c2pa2024, qwen2.5, rennie2005


- Mismatches are mostly minor issues like author ordering or year discrepancies in alemohammad2024_mad, garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded, he2021_deberta_v3, llama3, and guo2024_biscope. The not found entries for mitchell2023_detectgpt and liu2019_roberta are likely just OpenAlex lookup limitations since these are well-established papers, while knowledge_collapse2025 and falahati2026_curated might be recent preprints, and c2pa2024 is a specification rather than a traditional paper.

Now looking at the full review structure. The paper has solid strengths: it introduces recursive generation depth as an ordinal classification problem with a comprehensive 180K-sample benchmark across multiple models and strategies, includes extensive ablations and generalization tests, provides honest limitations, contributes the EDD metric, demonstrates that binary detectors fail at ordinal depth, and cites 67 references thoroughly. But there's a significant novelty concern—the authors themselves frame this as an empirical study and problem formalization rather than an algorithmic contribution, and the method relies on Random Forest with 19 hand-crafted features drawn from standard text analysis techniques like perplexity statistics, surprisal, lexical diversity, and repetition patterns.

The core question becomes whether problem formalization plus empirical validation alone meets the bar for EMNLP main conference. Beyond that, there's a critical scalability issue: the primary results showing 69-86% accuracy only hold for 1-1.5B parameter models, but at 14B the approach completely breaks down with EDD dropping to zero and accuracy falling to 54.1%. Since the largest and most consequential models in practice are 70B+ parameters and beyond, this severely undermines real-world applicability. The ecological validity gap is also substantial—the controlled LoRA fine-tuning setup on Wikipedia doesn't reflect how recursive generation actually happens in the wild, where contamination involves mixed corpora, varying proportions, multiple models, paraphrasing, and editing. While the authors acknowledge this limitation, they don't bridge it.

The metric presentation obscures the actual performance picture. The d0 recall exceeding 97% inflates the headline accuracy numbers, whereas the more honest d1-d3 balanced accuracy tells a different story: 71.6% within-distribution but only 55.4% cross-model, and a concerning 45.9% cross-strategy (barely above the 33% chance baseline). The cross-strategy failure is particularly problematic because the d1/d2 boundary inverts under cross-strategy transfer, meaning without knowing the decoding strategy used, the method can perform worse than random guessing on the most practical distinction. In real deployment scenarios, the generator's decoding strategy is typically unknown. Additionally, accuracy varies by up to 11 percentage points depending on which reference model is chosen, and since the actual generator is unknown in deployment, reference model selection becomes arbitrary.

The claimed utility for downstream applications isn't actually demonstrated. The curation proof-of-concept in the appendix shows no significant difference between the filtered and unfiltered results (p>0.4), undermining the paper's claim about enabling depth-graduated curation. The abstract is also problematic—it's seven sentences crammed with numbers that read more like a results dump than a coherent narrative, and the discussion section is essentially just a conclusion paragraph rather than substantive engagement with the implications.

Beyond the structural issues, there's a novelty question worth considering. The task formalization and EDD metric are genuinely new contributions, and the Depth Degradation Atlas provides useful empirical data, but the core method is fairly straightforward. The related work covers model collapse thoroughly and addresses AI text detection and ordinal classification adequately, though there's room to expand on data contamination detection beyond just model collapse.

Now I'm checking the abstract word count and reviewing the exact performance metrics to make sure I'm capturing the results accurately. I'm noticing the results section is extremely dense—packed with performance metrics and cross-validation numbers that make it hard to extract the core findings. The Discussion and Conclusion feel underdeveloped, merged into a single thin paragraph when they deserve more space to interpret what these depth signals actually mean for model behavior and future research directions. I'm settling on my final scores: Soundness at 3.5 out of 5 since the methodology is solid but there's a meaningful gap in ecological validity, Excitement at 2.5 out of 5 because while the task formulation is genuinely novel, the practical applicability is limited at this scale, and an Overall score of 3.0 positioning this as Findings-level work rather than main conference material—the empirical investigation is thorough and honest about limitations, but the lack of algorithmic innovation and scalability concerns hold it back. I'm confident in this assessment at 4 out of 5.
